{{For|a Gödel constructive set|Constructible universe}}
In [[topology]], '''constructible sets''' are a class of subsets of a [[topological space]] that have a relatively "simple" structure.
They are used particularly in [[algebraic geometry]] and related fields. A key result known as ''Chevalley's theorem''
in algebraic geometry shows that the image of a constructible set is constructible for an important class of [[map (mathematics)|mappings]]
(more specifically [[morphism of schemes|morphisms]]) of [[algebraic varieties]] (or more generally [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]]).
In addition, a large number of "local" geometric properties of schemes, morphisms and sheaves are (locally) constructible.
Constructible sets also feature in the definition of various types of [[constructible sheaf|constructible sheaves]] in algebraic geometry
and [[intersection cohomology]].

==Definitions==

A simple definition, adequate in many situations, is that a constructible set is a finite [[union (set theory)|union]] of [[locally closed set]]s. (A set is locally closed if it is the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of an [[open set]] and [[closed set]].) 
However, a modification and another slightly weaker definition are needed to have definitions that behave better with "large" spaces:

'''Definitions:''' A subset <math>Z</math> of a topological space <math>X</math> is called ''retrocompact'' if <math>Z\cap U</math> is [[compact space|compact]] for every compact open subset <math>U\subset X</math>. A subset of <math>X</math> is ''constructible'' if it is a ''finite'' union of subsets of the form <math>U\cap (X - V)</math> where both <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> are open ''and retrocompact'' subsets of <math>X</math>. 
A subset <math>Z\subset X</math> is ''locally constructible'' if there is a [[cover (topology)|cover]] <math>(U_i)_{i\in I}</math> of <math>X</math> consisting of open subsets with the property that each <math>Z\cap U_i</math> is a constructible subset of <math>U_i</math>. 
<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1961|loc= Ch. '''0'''<sub>III</sub>, Définitions (9.1.1), (9.1.2) and (9.1.11), pp. 12-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition 5.15.1 (tag 005G)|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/005G|access-date=2022-10-04|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref>

Equivalently the constructible subsets of a topological space <math>X</math> are the smallest collection <math>\mathfrak{C}</math> of subsets of <math>X</math> that (i) contains all open retrocompact subsets and (ii) contains all [[complement (set theory)|complements]] and finite unions (and hence also finite intersections) of sets in it. In other words, constructible sets are precisely the Boolean algebra generated by retrocompact open subsets.

In a [[locally noetherian topological space]], ''all'' subsets are retrocompact,<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1961|loc= Ch. '''0'''<sub>III</sub>, Sect. (9.1), p. 12}}</ref> and so for such spaces the simplified definition given first above is equivalent to the more elaborate one. Most of the commonly met schemes in algebraic geometry (including all [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]]) are locally Noetherian, but there are important constructions that lead to more general schemes.

In any (not necessarily [[noetherian space|noetherian]]) topological space, every constructible set contains a [[dense set|dense]] open subset of its closure.<ref>Jinpeng An (2012). [https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10711-011-9603-2 "Rigid geometric structures, isometric actions, and algebraic quotients"]. Geom. Dedicata '''157''': 153–185.</ref>

'''Terminology:''' The definition given here is the one used by the first edition of [[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA]] and the [[Stacks Project]]. In the second edition of EGA constructible sets (according to the definition above) are called "globally constructible" while the word "constructible" is reserved for what are called locally constructible above.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1971|loc= Ch. '''0'''<sub>I</sub>, Définitions (2.3.1), (2.3.2) and (2.3.10), pp. 55-57}}</ref>

==Chevalley's theorem==
A major reason for the importance of constructible sets in algebraic geometry is that the [[image (mathematics)|image]] of a (locally) constructible set is also (locally) constructible for a large class of maps (or "morphisms"). The key result is:

'''Chevalley's theorem.'''  If <math>f: X \to Y</math> is a [[Glossary of algebraic geometry#finite presentation|finitely presented]] morphism of schemes and <math>Z\subset X</math> is a locally constructible subset, then <math>f(Z)</math> is also locally constructible in <math>Y</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1964|loc= Ch. '''I''', Théorème (1.8.4), p. 239.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Theorem 29.22.3 (Chevalley's Theorem) (tag 054K) | url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054K|access-date=2022-10-04|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1971|loc= Ch. '''I''', Théorème (7.1.4), p. 329.}}</ref>

In particular, the image of an algebraic variety need not be a variety, but is (under the assumptions) always a constructible set. For example, the map <math>\mathbf A^2 \rightarrow \mathbf A^2</math> that sends <math>(x,y)</math> to <math>(x,xy)</math> has image the set <math>\{ x \neq 0 \} \cup \{ x=y=0 \}</math>, which is not a variety, but is constructible.

Chevalley's theorem in the generality stated above would fail if the simplified definition of constructible sets (without restricting to ''retrocompact'' open sets in the definition) were used.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Section 109.24 Images of locally closed subsets (tag 0GZL) | url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GZL | access-date=2022-10-04 | website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref>

==Constructible properties==
A large number of "local" properties of morphisms of schemes and [[quasicoherent sheaf|quasicoherent sheaves]] on schemes hold true over a locally constructible subset. EGA IV § 9<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1966|loc= Ch. '''IV''', § 9 Propriétés constructibles, pp. 54-94.}}</ref> covers a large number of such properties. Below are some examples (where all references point to EGA IV):
* If <math>f \colon X \rightarrow S</math> is a finitely presented morphism of schemes and <math>\mathcal{F}'\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}''</math> is a sequence of finitely presented quasi-coherent <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-modules, then the set of <math>s\in S</math> for which <math>\mathcal{F}'_s\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_s\rightarrow\mathcal{F}''_s</math> is [[exact sequence|exact]] is locally constructible. (Proposition (9.4.4))
* If <math>f \colon X \rightarrow S</math> is an finitely presented morphism of schemes and <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is a finitely presented quasi-coherent <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-module, then the set of <math>s\in S</math> for which <math>\mathcal{F}_s</math> is locally free is locally constructible. (Proposition (9.4.7))
* If <math>f \colon X \rightarrow S</math> is an finitely presented morphism of schemes and <math>Z\subset X</math> is a locally constructible subset, then the set of <math>s\in S</math> for which <math>f^{-1}(s)\cap Z</math> is closed (or open) in <math>f^{-1}(s)</math> is locally constructible. (Corollary (9.5.4))
* Let <math>S</math> be a scheme and <math>f \colon X \rightarrow Y</math> a morphism of <math>S</math>-schemes. Consider  the set <math>P\subset S</math> of <math>s\in S</math> for which the induced morphism <math>f_s\colon X_s\rightarrow Y_s</math> of fibres over <math>s</math> has some property <math>\mathbf{P}</math>. Then <math>P</math> is locally constructible if <math>\mathbf{P}</math> is any of the following properties<nowiki>:</nowiki> surjective, [[proper morphism|proper]], [[finite morphism|finite]], immersion, closed immersion, open immersion, isomorphism. (Proposition (9.6.1))
* Let <math>f \colon X \rightarrow S</math> be an finitely presented morphism of schemes and  consider  the set <math>P\subset S</math> of <math>s\in S</math> for which the fibre <math>f^{-1}(s)</math> has a property <math>\mathbf{P}</math>. Then <math>P</math> is locally constructible if <math>\mathbf{P}</math> is any of the following properties<nowiki>:</nowiki> [[geometrically (algebraic geometry)|geometrically]] irreducible, geometrically connected, geometrically reduced. (Theorem (9.7.7))
*Let <math>f \colon X \rightarrow S</math> be an locally finitely presented morphism of schemes and  consider  the set <math>P\subset X</math> of <math>x\in X</math> for which the fibre <math>f^{-1}(f(x))</math> has a property <math>\mathbf{P}</math>. Then <math>P</math> is locally constructible if <math>\mathbf{P}</math> is any of the following properties<nowiki>:</nowiki> geometrically regular, geometrically normal, geometrically reduced. (Proposition (9.9.4))

One important role that these constructibility results have is that in most cases assuming the morphisms in questions are also 
[[flat morphism|flat]] it follows that the properties in question in fact hold in an ''open'' subset. A substantial number of such results is included in EGA IV § 12.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1966|loc= Ch. '''IV''', § 12 Étude des fibres des morphismes plats de présentation finie, pp. 173-187.}}</ref>
